title: The Light of Christ
english: The darkness of night brings delight to those who are consumed by its shadows, and they cannot endure the gloom of evening. However, they attempt to drive away the darkness by filling their homes with lamps, and the light from these lamps chases away the shadows. For us, though, it is not a handmade light, nor a lamp with a moderate flame, that dispels the darkness, but Christ himself, who declares, 'I am the light of the world.' This is a truth that was also foretold by the prophet Isaiah, who cried out, 'Jerusalem, be enlightened, for your light has come.' The grace of our Savior has shone upon us, illuminating all things and dispelling the gloomy cloud of ignorance that had settled over us.

The devil had spread this cloud of ignorance over humanity, preventing anyone from lifting their heart's eye to what is pure and measuring the power of the Creator from the beauty of His creations. But now, those who were deceived have found great benefit in coming to know the truth. The devil had hoped to prevent them from gaining anything that would lead to salvation and rising to the freedom that is their birthright, but he has failed in his endeavor. For the One who calls us to salvation is greater than the devil, and a great multitude of people has been saved and has come to know their Creator, even if it was late in coming.

Those who were being instructed by the law towards knowledge of our Savior Jesus Christ, and the Jews who were being instructed by the doctrines through Moses, failed to recognize the Word of God who became human for us. As it is written, they abandoned the ways of their own vineyard, and the axles of their own tiller were plundered. The prophet Jeremiah strongly rebukes them, saying, 'How can you say, "We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us?"' For the scribes' false pen has worked in vain, and they were ashamed, impoverished, and captured.

What wisdom is in them, since they rejected the Word of the Lord? They truly rejected the only-begotten Word of God, but he has become the head of the corner. The prophet says somewhere about them, 'The sons are foolish and not intelligent.' How does it not seem true to everyone that what was said about them is true? They have become so neglectful of their own salvation that they do not even equal the efforts of the Gentiles in this regard. God says somewhere to them, 'I set watchmen over you, and I said, "Listen to the sound of the trumpet," and I said, "We will not listen." Therefore, the nations heard, and the shepherds of the flocks among them.

Hear, earth, for I am bringing evil upon this people, the fruit of their own food, because they have not attended to my law and have rejected my word. This rejection is not just a passive disregard, but an active refusal to follow the preaching of the holy apostles and to pay attention to the older books. If they were truly concerned about being benefited, they should not have allowed their minds to be deceived by the name of law, but rather should have examined the things concerning the Savior through the holy ones, and also the things said by others in figures and types.

One can see many images of things in the spiritual words, having a clear representation of our Savior's presence in the scripture. My mind is filled with various theories and memories of the holy Scripture, and I am compelled to consider the beginning of the word to be from the older things. Through the things that will make us more ready to believe, we should already proceed. Let us examine the diet of Abraham and how and in what things the blessed Abraham existed, and let the threefold birth and sowing of Isaac be investigated.

As we consider the story of Abraham and Sarah, we see the root of the nation and the mystery concerning our Savior, which is well and skillfully formed like bronze. The explanation of this mystery is found in the writings of Moses, and it is clearly unfolded in the history of the people. By examining this history, we can gain a deeper understanding of the events that transpired. Sarah, the wife of Abraham, was joined to him according to the law, but she was barren and had no children. Abraham, being eighty years old, had likely reached the end of his childbearing years, and the heat of nature for procreation had cooled in him.

Despite this, Sarah's desire for children remained strong, and she was burdened by her sorrow. She urged her husband to have relations with their maidservant, Hagar, an Egyptian woman, since she had not been deemed worthy of legitimate children. This decision was motivated by Sarah's love of children and her desire to have a family. The divine Scripture records this event, stating that Sarah, Abraham's wife, did not bear him children, but he had an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar, and Sarah said to Abraham...

The Lord had closed Sarah's womb, preventing her from bearing children. She told Abraham to enter into a relationship with her servant, so that he might have a child through her. However, this was not a matter of Sarah being persuaded to indulge in pleasure or being led into intemperance through her words to the patriarch. Rather, she was concerned about her inability to bear children, which she found difficult and burdensome. Such was Sarah's attitude towards her husband, and this plan was being led to its end by the patriarch. As a result, a child named Ishmael was born to Abraham from the Egyptian woman.

Meanwhile, Sarah's desires for a child were being deceived, and she thought that she would rejoice greatly in genuine childbirth. However, she was overcome with grief because she was unable to bear children. But God, the provider of all good hope and the one who has power over all things, had mercy on her and made the barren and childless woman fertile and suitable for childbirth. He then spoke to Abraham, saying, 'Your wife Sarah will no longer be called Sarah, but her name will be Sarah. I will bless her and give you a child from her, and I will bless that child. And that child will become a nation, and kings of nations will come from him.' Upon hearing this, Abraham fell on his face and laughed, saying to himself…

When Abraham was a hundred years old, would he have a son, and would Sarah, at the age of ninety, give birth? God spoke to Abraham, saying, 'Yes, indeed, your wife Sarah will bear a son, and you will name him Isaac.' This promise, made to Abraham, was a genuine one. As the events that had been announced reached their fulfillment, and the barren woman had learned to give birth, the child was already in sight, and the heir of the paternal household was apparent. Consequently, the maid, who had a non-legitimate son from Abraham, Ishmael, was being driven away as no longer needed.

As she fled, and had already become very far from her own home, an angel from heaven called out to her, saying, 'Hagar, maid of Sarah, where are you going?' And she replied, 'I am fleeing from the face of my mistress Sarah…'

title: Allegory of Abraham's Sons
english: The angel instructs her to humble herself under her mistress's hands, and although the story requires a longer account, it has been summarized for us. Now, we are left to contemplate the image of our Savior, for whom this broad word has been spoken to us.

The divine Paul, in his concise manner, has brought together a catalog of long accounts into one theory, transforming the unattractive thing into a more charming image of things. He writes to someone, saying that the law should not be despised, for it is written that Abraham had two sons, one from a slave and one from a free woman. These two sons are allegorized as two covenants, one from Mount Sinai, which gives birth to slavery, and the other from the free woman, which is our mother, the heavenly Jerusalem. Mount Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, and it corresponds to the present-day Jerusalem, which is in bondage with its children.

The nature of humanity, represented by Abraham, is the most ancient and fertile, having lived for a long time. It is a free nature, created by God, and has been allotted to rule all things. However, it has no genuine and God-given child, and instead delights in alien and illegitimate children, namely those from Egypt, a place of darkness. This darkness is interpreted as the false wisdom of the world, under which the ancient wise men were born. They were sons of the age, but illegitimate, and were raised as servants, serving gods not by nature.

As time has grown old and is coming to an end, the Son promised has been given, and human nature, which is idle and useless, like nothing, barren and childless, has given birth to a noble child, one of the chosen from the many. The heir, our Lord Jesus Christ, has appeared, and the servant girl is cast out with her children. Jacob had twelve children, some of whom numbered ten plus two.
The question arises, where is the wise man, the scribe, the debater of this age, for God has made foolish the wisdom of the world.

The one from the free woman still inherits, and the Father says to the Son, ask and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession. A divine goodness does not allow the cast-out servant girl to perish with her children; instead, she is sent back and told to humble herself under the hands of the free woman. The false wisdom of the world, which once mocked the marriages of the free, now serves the noble children of God through the most noble agreement of words, serving divine spectacles. The birth of Isaac from the promise signifies nothing other than the birth of Christ at the end of the ages. Let no one be troubled if not all parts of the story are applied to the truth, for allegorical interpretations are introduced against the possible meanings.

The righteous is often compared to a sheep due to the gentleness inherent in the animal. However, it is completely unbelievable to suggest that the righteous would engage in aggressive behavior, such as goring or butting with horns. Instead, we must focus on the demonstration of the things at hand, for it is necessary for Christ to appear in the generation according to Isaac, as if formed through a type. By examining the divine Scripture, we can gain a deeper understanding of the truth and avoid using superfluous and idle words.

God did not make the promise to Abraham for the sake of anyone else, but for the sake of our Savior's sojourn, on which the conclusion of the blessing depends. As the divine word declares, 'I will bless her, and I will give you a child from her, and I will bless him, and he will be for nations, and kings of nations will come out from him.' (Genesis 17:16) The covenant is eternal, and its conclusion is tied to the sojourn of our Savior. It is clear that Isaac became the father of one son, Jacob, and the blessed Jacob sprang only from him; and Jacob had twelve children, but only one tribe, that of the Jews, was given from them.

The statement 'It will be for the nations' will be fulfilled when the nation from Israel, although divided into twelve tribes, is still considered one nation, composed of many members, but filled into one body through all. This is because the covenant defined through Moses is not an eternal covenant from God to those from the seed of Isaac. The prophet Joel announces that God will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah (Joel 2:28), which Paul understands well.

Paul explains that when God says 'new', he has made the first covenant old, and the old and aging one is near disappearance. Therefore, there has been an annulment of the previous command, and an introduction of a better hope, through which we approach God. It has been demonstrated that Abraham, who is from one nation, has become the father of many nations, and it is necessary to bring Christ into the promise. He was the one depicted in that passage, and he has become the father of many nations, drawing all to himself through faith, and rejoicing in the multitude of nations. Let Paul, the wisest, also be a witness to the truth, and let him struggle together with me, saying that the promise of God is fulfilled in Christ.

The one who supplies the Spirit to you and works powers in you does so not because of your works of law, but because of your hearing of faith, just as Abraham believed God and was reckoned to him for righteousness (Galatians 3:6). This is why you know that those who are from faith are the true sons of Abraham. The power of the promise, therefore, will be for those who are not just born according to the flesh, but for those who, through their faith in Christ, are inscribed as children of Abraham.

The blessed Baptist said to those from Israel, when they were boasting about their fleshly connection and presenting Abraham as the ancestor of their race, 'Make fruits worthy of repentance, and do not think to say among yourselves, we have Abraham as our father.' (Matthew 3:9) For God can raise up children for Abraham from these stones.

title: Faith and Obedience
english: Those who are numb in mind are burdened as if with a heart, but if someone examines the Gentiles closely, they will find them to be such and no different, for they were raised through faith and became children of Abraham, and fellow heirs of Isaac, and sharers in the blessing on him.
Paul will testify to this, saying that the Scripture foretold that God justifies the Gentiles through faith, and that all nations will be blessed in Abraham (Genesis 12:3, 22:18).
The one who came from Abraham, Isaac, is formed into our Lord Jesus Christ (Genesis 22:2), and it can be shown from all sides, and very easily.

The promise to Abraham is fulfilled again in those who believe in Christ, and Paul will assure us of this, writing to the Galatians that no one annuls or adds to a ratified human covenant, but the promises were spoken to Abraham and his seed, and he does not say seeds as if many, but as one, and to his seed who is Christ (Galatians 3:16).
As many as were baptized into Christ put on Christ, and there is no distinction between Jew or Greek, slave or free, male or female, for you are all one in Jesus Christ (Galatians 3:27-28).
Therefore, you are the descendants of Abraham and heirs according to the promise.
The multitude of things said provides sufficient proof for the subject at hand.
However, if you think I have spoken too little, O Jew, and that my words are of no value, and you refuse to agree with us, then the blame lies not with me, but with your disobedience.

Those who strive to speak the most powerful words cannot be held responsible if they fail to persuade their listeners, for they have worked diligently to express what is within them, and thus they are free from blame.

On the other hand, those who listen to the best teachings and yet refuse to agree are guilty of the most shameful behavior, similar to one who receives a loan and proves to be ungrateful and ignorant, for such a person does not demonstrate the lender's evil, but rather their own.
By considering the experiences of doctors, I realize that their pursuit of the medical art is wise, and their discoveries about the sick are not outside the realm of sober reasoning.

Let us, therefore, imitate their approach and treat the stubborn with the same remedies, so to speak, for just as doctors restore the health of one who has fallen into sickness, if they see that the passions have taken you, they present a variety of restraints and order you to take what is sufficient from all sides, doing well.

The Jewish person, who has much foolishness as a disease, is invited to obey and follow the path of righteousness, and by looking at the story of Isaac, we can see a prefiguration of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Abraham, the renowned patriarch, was given a command by God that seemed harsh and paradoxical to some: to sacrifice his beloved son Isaac as a whole burnt offering (Genesis 22:2).
This command raises questions about the nature of God and the morality of such an action, for how could God advise Abraham to kill his own son, who was righteous and barely given to him in old age?

The patriarch's response to this command teaches us about the importance of obedience and trust in God's plan, for by silencing our own doubts and establishing a household management based on the announced, we can learn to trust in God's wisdom and vote against the inhumanity that can arise from our own foolishness.

God's commands are not meant to be harsh or inhumane, but rather to test our faith and trust in Him, as evident in the story of Abraham and Isaac, where God says, 'Take your beloved son, whom you loved, Isaac, and go to the high land and offer him as a whole burnt offering on one of the mountains that I will tell you' (Genesis 22:2).

Abraham, not neglecting the divine command, considered it more important than his affection for his child and obeyed, taking his son Isaac to the place God had told him, and after cutting wood for the burnt offering, he went to the place God had told him, on the third day.

From afar, Abraham saw the place and said to his servants, showing his trust in God's command, 'Sit with the donkey, I and the child will go as far as here, and having worshiped, we will return to you.', and then he took the wood for the burnt offering and put it on his son Isaac, and he also took the fire and the knife.

The two of them went together to the place that God had told him, where Abraham built an altar and arranged the wood on it, and then he bound Isaac and put him on the altar on top of the wood, stretching out his hand to take the knife and slaughter his son.

Just as Abraham was about to sacrifice Isaac, an angel of the Lord called out to him, saying 'Abraham, Abraham' (Genesis 22:11), and Abraham replied, 'Here I am.', and the angel then instructed him not to lay a hand on the child or do anything to him, saying 'Now I know that you fear God, and you have not withheld your beloved son from me.', and Abraham looked up and saw a ram caught in a thorn bush, which he then took and offered as a burnt offering instead of his son Isaac, thus fulfilling the divine command without sacrificing his child.

On the third day, he comes, having ordered two servants to follow him, and the fact that the child is carried to the sacrifice by the father symbolizes that it was not human power or the plotting of those who sought to harm him that led Jesus Christ to the cross, but rather the will of the Father, who allowed him to endure death for the sake of all.

The Savior also spoke to Pilate, saying that he had no authority over him unless it was given from above (John 19:11), and to the Father in heaven, saying, 'Father, if possible, let this cup pass from me, yet not as I will, but as you will' (Matthew 26:42)...
